Now today, whether you're leading school outreach, building university partnerships, running a counseling practice, or growing an educational venture, TOC is the space where education professionals come together. We learn, we grow, we collaborate without barriers or any gatekeeping. And we're delighted to have you as a part of today's learning community.

Today's conclave, while we talk about creative careers, we'd love to talk about every career that goes beyond the traditional route. We've spoken about careers that power industries ranging from fashion, communication, digital media, and product innovation to, of course, sustainability. And what we are looking at is, despite the rapid growth, many students and families still remain unaware and relate that creative careers only with a handful of familiar options.

So today what we are doing is we're bringing to the table two diverse ideas. One where we'll be exploring: through Explore, we'll broaden our understanding of creative careers, the ecosystem, and building beyond conventional design. And for that, we have two very special panelists joining us today, and it's my pleasure and privilege to introduce our first panelist. Joining us today is Miss Emilie Li, Associate Director of Admission at Savannah College of Art and Design, or SCAD as we popularly know it, in the USA. Emilie is a passionate cross-functional marketing professional with a strong background in fashion marketing, luxury retail, and brings valuable industry experience as well. Having consistently achieved top sales goals while working in luxury fashion, she herself holds a degree in marketing and merchandising and is currently pursuing a Master's in Luxury Fashion Management. Beyond admissions, Emilie has experience in event planning, fashion, and modeling, bringing a unique perspective that connects creativity, business, and the industry together. As someone who works closely with aspiring creative students from around the world, Emilie has firsthand insights into the evolving landscape of creative education in international education. She's here today to help us explore, understand the expanding expanse of the vast arena of creative careers, and to understand the opportunities available to students across disciplines. Please join me in welcoming Miss Emilie Li. Emilie, the floor is yours.

Now, the newest addition to SCAD is Robotics and Music. Both of the programs are launching this fall, and we're constantly evolving our program to staying relevant to the creative industry. Now, I keep mentioning SCADpro. SCADpro is our collaborative innovation studio. It pairs our student with Fortune 500 companies in a classroom and help them build real industry projects. Now, we have done almost 900-plus projects. 75 of them, product or service, are being launched to the market. And this is just a great way for our student to get real industry experience. Now, SCADpro is a direct professional pathway to gain real industry experience. Outcome & Learning: End with the strongest photograph. The last slide of that particular project should be the final outcome, and that should look good. Space & Experience: Interior concepts, exhibition space, installations, retail environment, storytelling. Visual Communication: For all the students who are applying for industrial, communication, UI/UX, multimedia. They should also understand your knowledge and idea about your understanding about the world through your portfolio. That can also be one of the things.

So after attending so many critical feedbacks, after attending so many advisory sessions, what makes a portfolio strong? 1. Original Thinking: If there is no original thinking, trust me, it's not going to work out. You show a Ganga Ghat in Varanasi, a very beautiful painting. It can work, but you have to show why it is original. A personal point of view is more important than like a proper fashionable topic. "I have made artwork of Messi because I like football, so I made a portrait of Messi"—you cannot do that. You have to study the life of Messi, you have to study what he has all gone through, and in the colors, in the textures, in the print, you can use those things in the artwork. So the things cannot go just like that. Because I liked it, I made it—you have to explain why and why it is related with the course you are applying for, until unless you are not applying for a foundation year. 2. Clarity of Communication: Extremely important. The person who is checking your portfolio is not going to take more than 5 minutes of time for the portfolio you did 2 years or 2 and a half years to create. So the clarity of communication has to be there. It should not be confusing. The viewer should quickly understand the idea behind the portfolio. 3. Depth of Process: How much depth you have put in the process. 4. Range with Connection: Demonstrate with different skills and media. 5. Quality of Final Work: Quality of final work is extremely important. 6. Self-Aware Reflection: Explain decisions honestly, mention limitations, learning, future development rather than claiming that every experimentation was perfect.
